analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 50 or more workers to provide one to two weeks of paid vacation.
analysis.headline: The Paid Vacation Act never advanced: introduced in May 2013 with zero cosponsors, referred to committee, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to guarantee paid vacation for the first time in federal law. Employers with 100 or more workers would have to give each eligible employee one week of paid vacation right away, and two weeks after three years; employers with 50 or more workers would have to give one week after three years. Employees would need at least a year on the job and 1,250 hours worked, and would have to give 30 days' notice before taking the time. The Labor Department would also run a public awareness campaign and study how paid leave affects productivity and health.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of larger employers — firms with 50 or more workers — who currently get no guaranteed paid vacation under federal law. The United States is the only advanced economy that does not require any paid vacation, so many workers, especially in lower-wage jobs, get none at all. An estimated 1 in 4 private-sector workers lacks any paid vacation today. Employees would gain a week or two of paid time off, in a continuous block, that could not be rolled over or replaced by existing leave.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that, immediately upon passage, every employer with 100 or more employees must provide each eligible employee one workweek of paid vacation per 12-month period.

Beginning three years after passage, employers with 50 or more employees must provide one week of paid vacation, and employers with 100 or more must provide two weeks, starting on the employee's first work anniversary.
The vacation must be a continuous block of days, separate from sick leave and any other legally required leave, and cannot be rolled over or carried into the next year.
The Labor Department would run a public awareness campaign about the new entitlement and publish a study on the leave's effects on productivity, public health, and psychological well-being.
The bill overrides the small-business exemptions in FLSA Section 13 for this provision, so covered employers could not claim exemption from the vacation requirement.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees, who would pay wages for one to two weeks of vacation that workers currently do not take. Those costs would be borne in part through lower wage growth, higher prices, or reduced hiring at the margin. Workers with less than a year on the job or under 1,250 hours of service get nothing, and workers at firms under 50 employees are excluded entirely.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for covered employers — paying workers for time not worked — which an honest supporter would acknowledge could show up as slower wage growth, higher prices, or fewer hours, and business groups generally opposed any federal paid-leave mandate.

The bill leaves most workers out: employees need 12 months on the job and 1,250 hours of service to qualify, part-time workers often cannot reach that threshold, and workers at firms with fewer than 50 employees are never covered at all.
Workers must give at least 30 days' notice before taking vacation, which limits flexibility, and the vacation cannot be rolled over, so workers who cannot use it in a given year lose it.
The bill does not say what happens if an employer refuses to comply — there is no enforcement mechanism spelled out beyond the entitlement itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is straightforward: guaranteed, genuine paid time off in a country with no federal vacation requirement, worth roughly 1-2% of annual pay to covered employees plus the health and productivity benefits the bill itself would study. The costs are real but modest and phased in over three years, and the coverage limits (50-employee threshold, 12-month/1,250-hour requirement) mean many of the lowest-wage workers who most lack vacation get nothing. It is a meaningful but partial benefit, drawn narrowly enough that its main political weakness was leaving out so many workers while still imposing a mandate on employers.

outcome.mechanism: Rep. Grayson introduced it alone with no cosponsors; the House Education and the Workforce Committee referred it to a subcommittee, never acted on it, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the Paid Vacation Act in the House on May 22, 2013.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On July 8, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House over its entire life.
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 50 or more employees are better off, since they never had to fund the mandated vacation, and the requirement never took effect. Workers who lack paid vacation gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paid Vacation Act on May 22, 2013 and advocated for a federal paid vacation guarantee.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action beyond referring it to a subcommittee, where it died.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on July 8, 2013 and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: The House's 434 other members
against.what_they_did: Not one member of either party signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's two-year life, leaving it without a support base to move it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so it never attracted enough support to test whether the divide was partisan.

industries.note: The bill would require these firms to pay for one to two weeks of vacation per eligible employee, a direct payroll cost. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against workers who would have gained the paid leave.
Firms under the 50-employee threshold would be exempt entirely, putting them at a relative competitive advantage against covered larger firms, while their own workers would get no vacation guarantee.
Guaranteed vacation would channel more consumer spending into leisure travel, hotels, and recreation — an industry that generally benefits when workers get paid time off.
